    #187789. (Mis)judgments in Football Analysis (1/3) – MH

    📅 26 May 2025 • ⏱️ 29m • 📚 Deep Dive (5811 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Spielverlagerung ↗ Open Full Page

    (Mis)judgments in Football Analysis (1/3) – MH

    📅 26 May 2025 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 26.05.2025 in den Kategorien Uncategorized,Video Analysis mit 4 Kommentaren.
    • Industry observers note that daniel Kahneman was one of the leading psychologists of our time.
    • Kahneman became well known in the field of behavioral economics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 26.05.2025 in den Kategorien Uncategorized,Video Analysis mit 4 Kommentaren.

    Industry observers note that daniel Kahneman was one of the leading psychologists of our time. In his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, he presented extensive insights from his many years of research. This article explores how Kahneman’s findings, along with other insights from behavioral science, can be applied to (strategic and tactical) football analysis.

    Kahneman became well known in the field of behavioral economics. Together with his colleague Amos Tversky, he succeeded in combining insights from psychology with those of economics. In 2002, he became the first psychologist to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences.

    His research challenges the fundamental assumption that humans make rational decisions and that cognitive distortions are primarily driven by emotions. Instead, he argued that systematic thinking errors significantly influence our judgment and decision-making. These systematic errors, known as “biases,” occur in predictable ways under certain conditions.

    In a recent development, kahneman’s work has been applied in fields such as medical diagnosis, the legal system, intelligence analysis, philosophy, statistics, and military strategy. It is therefore a logical step to apply his research to sports analysis, where strategic decisions also play a crucial role.

    “I suppose that every author has in mind a situation in which readers of their work might benefit from reading it. I imagine the coffee machine at the office, where colleagues exchange opinions and gossip. My hope is to enrich the vocabulary people use when they talk about the judgments and decisions of others (…).” – Daniel Kahneman; Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    A mere list of cognitive biases is not sufficient to recognize and avoid distortions in one’s own or others’ decisions. Only through a deeper understanding of their origins and mechanisms can the vocabulary around judgment and decision-making be enriched in Kahneman’s sense. Therefore, this article sheds light on the underlying processes and mechanisms of judgment and decision errors.

    It has been revealed that we begin by examining the scientifically established dual-process model. Following that, the mechanisms of WYSIATI, substitution, and priming will be explored in the context of football. In addition, the most relevant heuristics and cognitive biases will be applied to football analysis. Finally, we will address individual factors within analysis that contribute to the emergence of bias.

    This article is only the first part of a series, which will span at least three essays. The series will examine flawed judgments in football analysis and their causes within a scientific framework informed by behavioral research.

    One point should be made clear from the outset: bias (and noise) are present wherever decisions are made, and thus affect even expert judgments within their domain.

    This article is based on a German translation of Daniel Kahneman’s work. Accordingly, the quotes cited here may not exactly match the original English wording.

    Recent findings suggest that to explain human thinking, Kahneman introduces two hypothetical agents: System 1 and System 2. This model provides a framework for understanding how thought processes work. System 1 is responsible for fast thinking, it operates automatically, intuitively, and with little effort. System 2, on the other hand, governs slow thinking, it works analytically, consciously, and requires effort.

    These two systems interact continuously whenever we are awake. System 1 runs constantly and automatically, while System 2 operates in an energy-saving mode, only stepping in occasionally. As a result, System 2 rarely takes control. Typically, System 2 adopts the impressions and intuitions generated by System 1 and accepts its intuitive responses.

    Recent findings suggest that the division of labor between the two systems is highly efficient. From an evolutionary perspective, this can be explained by the need to react promptly to threats while also engaging in deliberate, long-term planning. Thus, the automatic System 1 developed primarily for threat detection, while the energy-intensive System 2 evolved to support complex reasoning, though it is less frequently engaged in full.

    However, it is particularly System 1 that is susceptible to cognitive biases. Due to its energy efficiency, it is limited in logic and statistical reasoning. It often tends to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. System 2, in turn, tends to adopt these flawed outputs, as it does not always monitor or correct the conclusions generated by System 1.

    The following simple and intuitive thinking task illustrates the interplay between System 1 and System 2:.

    In a recent development, team A has 62% possession and wins a match 1-0. Team B has 38% possession and loses. Which team was more dominant?

    Recent findings suggest that of course, Team A was more dominant. At least, that’s the intuitive conclusion System 1 leads most people to. However, it neglects the fact that possession is not necessarily a reliable measure of dominance, and that match results are very imprecise indicators of performance. Despite lacking detailed data, System 1 assembles the question into a coherent picture. System 2 supports System 1’s incorrect solution, even though with minimal effort it could have reached the correct conclusion. However, System 2 is not consciously engaged.

    From this, it follows that people rely on mental shortcuts, so-called heuristics, to rapidly solve complex problems. Heuristics are usually very helpful due to their efficiency but can sometimes lead to errors in judgment, known as biases. This is where the relevance for football analysis arises, as will be shown in the following section.

    “A heuristic is, technically defined, a simple procedure that helps us find adequate, though often imperfect, answers to difficult questions.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    First, I have linked a YouTube video that you should watch:.

    According to recent reports, even if you are already familiar with the video, its insights are remarkable. On the one hand, it can be concluded that focusing on one task can make us blind to other processes. To see and orient ourselves, we need a certain level of attention. However, the main insight of the video is that we cannot believe we have missed something so obvious. For those who did not see the gorilla, the player leaving the scene, or the curtain changing colors, it is unimaginable not to have noticed such obvious events.

    “We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Applied to our football analysis, this once again demonstrates how prone we are to errors. How can we direct our attention to all levels of football tactics when, at the slightest distraction, we don’t even see a gorilla? We are only just beginning to discover many additional dimensions of the game as reference points, alongside spatial considerations in positional play. It is not only individual situations that are overlooked due to lack of attention, but possibly entire dimensions and we may not even be aware of this.

    Recent findings suggest that we only realize our mistakes when we can no longer analyze a team with the tools we have. We follow our own subjective beliefs in analysis and overlook other logical conclusions that could have been drawn equally well from the existing data. This problem becomes particularly interesting when assessing tactical risk.

    Industry observers note that recall the earlier question where you were asked to judge a team’s dominance based on possession percentages and the match result. System 1 constructed the best story it could from high possession and a win. What was not done, however, was likely questioning what is necessary to authentically assess a team’s dominance. We are blind to what we do not pay attention to.

    Recent findings suggest that hasty conclusions based on limited data form the basis of many heuristics. Kahneman refers to these conclusions as “What You See Is All There Is” (WYSIATI).

    “It is easier to fit everything you know into a coherent pattern when you know very little.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    This central mechanism explains why consistency of information, rather than its completeness, is what primarily shapes our beliefs. Unfortunately, we also interpret information accordingly through our coherence-seeking System 1. Kahneman explains that System 1 is completely insensitive to the quality and quantity of information from which impressions and intuitions arise. System 1 looks for coherent information, while a lazy System 2 fails to check it.

    According to recent reports, “They did not want more information that might spoil their story. WYSIATI.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    To start, I have prepared a question that should first be answered:.

    How successful will Relationism be compared to Positionism in the next ten years in the top 5 leagues?

    The answer will follow at the end of this section….

    It has been revealed that to interpret actions and processes, a complex, multidimensional understanding of the game is necessary. In analysis, we face difficult questions that can be answered on multiple levels. Often, there is not just one correct analysis, but several possibilities which together create an accurate picture.

    “I know that I know nothing.” (cf. Plato, Apology 22d: “For I was conscious that I knew practically nothing…” ).

    Through reflection and the constant questioning of our observations and conclusions, we come closer to the goal of better understanding the game. The ability to accept that there are always latest perspectives and interpretations fosters a deeper, more nuanced understanding. Unfortunately, when faced with complex matters, humans intuitively tend to fall into different patterns of thinking.

    Recent findings suggest that kahneman explains that even with complex questions, we rarely seem overwhelmed. We are able to provide answers to questions we do not fully understand. But why is that?

    According to recent reports, heuristics, as explained above, can be defined as mental shortcuts. Unfortunately, complex questions must also be answered in an energy-efficient way. Thus, we tend to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. This concept underlying many heuristics is called substitution. Often, we do not even notice that we have replaced a difficult question. However, we then use the answer to the simpler question to respond to the complex one. System 1 strives for the simplest possible answer to a question, while System 2, due to its inertia, does not verify the answer.

    “You are not overwhelmed, you don’t have to exert much effort, and you may not even notice that you have not answered the question that was asked of you.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    The concept of substitution is particularly pronounced when emotions are involved in the actual target question. Emotional attitudes amplify the effect. In the case of the so-called affect heuristic (judgments based on emotions), the interaction between System 1 and System 2 is especially prone to disruption. In the context of emotions and attitudes, System 2 does not act as a self-critic but rather as an advocate for the answer proposed by System 1. It looks for arguments that support its own beliefs.

    According to recent reports, let us return to the question posed at the beginning of this section. You most likely found an answer to how successful Relationismus will be in the future. However, instead of systematically thinking through the target question, an answer intuitively came to you that corresponds to your beliefs. The heuristic question you unconsciously answered might have been: How much do I like Guardiola’s Positionismus?

    It has been revealed that instead of searching for counterarguments against the intuitive answer, you subsequently searched for arguments that support your beliefs. To make a reliable future prediction, it would actually be necessary to free oneself from prejudices and break down the problem into its components, systematically questioning in which situations relational play is superior to positional play and in which situations the opposite is true. After all, the two philosophies can also be combined.

    It can be concluded that substitution, together with WYSIATI, forms two of the most crucial mechanisms in the interplay of System 1 and System 2 underlying many systematic cognitive errors. The following section will introduce another mechanism: priming.

    Priming is a fundamental mechanism that explains how we process information when thinking. Our memory plays a central role in this, more precisely, the way it connects information. This principle is called association.

    Kahneman uses a metaphor to explain association: “Like ripples on the surface of a pond, activation spreads through a small part of the vast network of associated representations.” Even a single stimulus can be enough to unconsciously activate adjacent concepts or memories.

    According to recent reports, A priming effect occurs when a specific stimulus, a word, an image, a situation, etc. unconsciously activates certain content in memory. This automatic chain of activation influences how we think, feel, or act without us noticing. The brain essentially lays down mental pathways in the associative network, thereby facilitating the unconscious retrieval of information.

    Recent findings suggest that to illustrate, here is a simple example: “If you have recently seen or heard the word eat, you will be temporarily more likely to complete the word fragment so_p as soup rather than soap. The opposite would happen if you had just seen the word wash.”– Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Priming is already being used effectively in football contexts. For example, tactical training that includes video analysis and corresponding training formats represents a form of priming. By showing (tactical) videos during team meetings or recreating game-like patterns in training sessions, players can recognize familiar situations during matches, allowing them to react more promptly and effectively. Training decision-making under pressure and developing speed of action can therefore be linked to the priming effect.

    Sources indicate that another well-known example of this effect is the “Florida effect.” For those interested in reading more, I’ve linked the original 1996 study by John A. Bargh, Mark Chen, and Lara Burrows.

    Priming also plays a role in many other areas of football. It can be deliberately used to create positive outcomes, but it can also have unintended negative effects. Depending on the context, different types of priming are distinguished, such as semantic priming, affective priming, goal priming, and many more. In football, priming is also used, for example, in injury prevention and rehabilitation.

    Priming can also be used for the cognitive preparation of a match. In the so-called “Moments of Excellence,” players consciously recall their best past performances immediately before a game. Particularly interesting is the application of “success priming” by the coach, through the use of specific words or phrases in the pre-match talk. Attached is a 2006 study by Stajkovic, Locke, and Blair on this topic, specifically on the unconscious performance enhancement through goal activation.

    According to recent reports, analysts, too, are subject to unconscious priming. A glance at the final score before conducting an analysis primes their expectations and subtly shifts the approach toward explaining the outcome, even though the final score, due to its inaccuracy as a performance indicator, says little about a team’s actual dominance.

    Given the scope of the subject, an entire article could likely be written solely on the use of priming in football. In this article, however, the foundations of priming are used to understand it as one of the mechanisms underlying cognitive biases that affect football analysis.

    “They were primed to find flaws, and that is exactly what they found.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    It has been revealed that note: An earlier version mentioned the so-called “Florida Effect.” This belongs to a group of priming phenomena that, in the context of the replication crisis, have been only weakly or not at all confirmed. Those interested in learning more can find further information in the comment section. Many thanks to “AG” for the attentive feedback!

    Recent findings suggest that at the beginning of the introduction, I explained that distortions in our thinking and decision-making occur in predictable ways under certain conditions. By now, you should have developed a basic understanding of how our thinking is governed by the interaction between System 1 and System 2, how intuitive judgments arise in the process of analysis, and how mechanisms such as WYSIATI, substitution, and priming can specifically contribute to systematic biases in football analysis.

    In a recent development, so far, around 200 cognitive biases have been identified. However, unlike many other articles that present a long list of biases with only brief descriptions, I deliberately refrain from doing so here. In my view, a simple enumeration does little to help recognize or avoid these distortions in practice. Instead, I focus on a small number of key biases that are particularly relevant to football analysis. Part 2 of this series will examine additional biases in the context of overconfidence.

    Recent findings suggest that “Coherence means that you’re going to adopt one interpretation in general. Ambiguity tends to be suppressed. This is part of the mechanism that you have here that ideas activate other ideas and the more coherent they are, the more likely they are to activate to each other. Other things that don’t fit fall by the wayside. We’re enforcing coherent interpretation. We see the world as much more coherent than it is.” – Daniel Kahneman, Edge.

    What Kahneman describes here is the phenomenon called associative coherence. The processing of subjectively fitting information is facilitated by associative memory, while the processing of mismatching information is hindered. System 1 thus generates a coherent pattern of activated ideas in associative memory.

    Recent findings suggest that this phenomenon inevitably leads to errors in analysis. We should be aware that our analysis alone will never capture the entirety of the subject being analyzed. The analysis is always an expression of the analyst’s beliefs and the ideas activated in their associative memory. Even though System 2 can counteract when activated, it is still influenced by System 1. The concept of associative coherence is therefore closely related to WYSIATI and priming.

    As part of the outcome of associative coherence, confirmation bias can be seen. It describes our tendency to want to confirm our existing beliefs.

    Sources indicate that “The coherence of associative activation induces a confirmatory bias when people examine a hypothesis by increasing the accessibility of hypothesis-consistent information. For example, the intention to test the proposition that ‘Sam is friendly‘ preferentially activates evidence of Sam’s friendliness, whereas testing the proposition that ‘Sam is not friendly‘ preferentially evokes instances of hostile behavior.” – Associative Processes in Intuitive Judgement.

    Industry observers note that in analysis, we tend to seek out, select, and interpret information in a way that confirms our expectations. This, of course, applies to all areas of football analysis. Active countermeasures are necessary to avoid overlooking data that contradicts one’s own hypothesis.

    To simplify the illustration of anchoring, please answer the following two questions one after the other.

    Does Cristiano Ronaldo have more or less than 1,200 international matches for the senior national team?

    How many international matches for the senior national team has Cristiano Ronaldo played?

    Recent findings suggest that you have very likely come to the conclusion that Ronaldo has played fewer than 1,200 international matches. Nevertheless, this value probably influenced your estimate of the second question towards a number that is too high. Ronaldo has (as of March 2025) played 219 international matches.

    According to recent reports, judgments are often based on the first piece of information given, the anchor. This biases the estimate in its direction. Daniel Kahneman distinguishes two psychological mechanisms that explain this effect.

    Sources indicate that the anchoring effect is measured and demonstrated in most psychological studies using numerical estimates, for example by estimating prices or probabilities. However, such quantitative judgments are not directly present in video analysis in football. To nevertheless apply the anchoring effect to this context, a change of perspective is useful: Richards J. Heuer Jr., among others a former CIA analyst, investigated the influence of cognitive biases, including the anchoring effect, on qualitative judgment processes within the intelligence community. In his book Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, Heuer deliberately does not refer only to mere numerical estimates, but to all kinds of ongoing judgments or assessments that an analyst inherits from predecessors or gradually revises themselves. Empirical evidence for the effectiveness of anchoring effects in sports video analysis is still lacking, but an analogy via the intelligence community is plausible.

    Industry observers note that as already described above, the match result provides the analyst with the first available piece of information, acting as a kind of anchor. A 4–0 or 2–1 score leads us to attribute tactical superiority to the winning team and to base our tactical assessments too strongly on the result.

    “We should, in any case, assume that every number presented to us has an anchoring effect on us (…).” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Another example of an anchoring effect in video analysis can be found when analyzing multiple matches of a team. The first game analyzed sets an initial assessment of the team’s tactical approach. As the analysis progresses, the analyst may need to revise their judgments but often fails to adjust sufficiently and remains primarily anchored to the initial assessment. This results in a biased analysis skewed toward the anchor game.

    „Even when analysts make their own initial judgment, and then attempt to revise this judgment on the basis of new information or further analysis, there is much evidence to suggest that they usually do not change the judgment enough.” – Psychology of Intelligence Analysis.

    It is not surprising that people look for reference points when faced with complex concerns, the anchor provides exactly this orientation. Unfortunately, in certain cases, it distorts our decision-making. Mussweiler and Strack investigated in their study “Overcoming the Inevitable Anchoring Effect: Considering the Opposite Compensates for Selective Accessibility” how the anchoring effect can be mitigated. Simply being aware of the anchor and the effect is unfortunately not enough to avoid the bias. Instead, a strategy of deliberately thinking about the opposite proves effective in preventing it. Imagine, instead of a 4–0 victory, a 0–4 defeat, and consider how your analysis would look in that case.

    Recent findings suggest that outcome Bias describes the tendency to judge performance based on the outcome. It is closely related to the principle of anchoring. The result serves as an anchor that shifts the judgment in its direction.

    Sources indicate that unlike the example mentioned above regarding bias from the match result, Outcome Bias can be applied to all types of results. This means that individual actions and sequences by players are evaluated based on their success or failure, regardless of the actual quality of execution.

    An example of this is a successful pressing sequence that leads to winning the ball. Because of the positive outcome, the pressing is overall rated as good. However, other relevant factors, such as intensity, timing, the opponent’s reaction, etc. are either not considered at all or only insufficiently taken into account.

    According to recent reports, if the same pressing sequence is executed again in a different game situation but fails to win the ball, the pressing is suddenly rated as poor, even though the execution was identical. This bias demonstrates how strongly the evaluation is influenced by the outcome rather than by the quality of the action itself. All actions in the game can be subject to Outcome Bias in analysis.

    To prevent Outcome Bias, the evaluation criteria should be adjusted. Instead of judging a performance by its outcome, the process quality should be assessed. This increases the likelihood of future successful actions.

    According to recent reports, the availability heuristic describes a cognitive shortcut in which people assess the frequency or likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind. In doing so, the original question: “How often does an event occur?” is replaced by a simpler one: “How easily can I recall relevant examples?”. This is a typical example of the substitution mechanism.

    It has been revealed that more key for the availability of an action than the number of examples one can recall is how easily they come to mind, what is known as ease of retrieval. A paradoxical example illustrating the effect of the availability heuristic was demonstrated by Schwarz et al. in 1991: people are less convinced by a decision when asked to list as many arguments in favor of it as possible. This approach plays the two factors, number of arguments and ease of retrieval, against each other: the more arguments that must be generated, the harder they are to retrieve.

    In a recent development, in the context of football analysis, this heuristic can lead to an overestimation of certain in-game actions or patterns, particularly during live matches. Striking, prominent, or emotional moments are more easily remembered and therefore disproportionately influence our overall evaluation of the game, regardless of how frequent or relevant they actually were. The availability heuristic has a particularly strong impact on our perception of risk (explored in Part 2).

    In a recent development, the game scenes most readily accessible to the analyst are also heavily influenced by their subjective experiences. A wide range of impressions, such as those from previous roles, past matches, or preferred playing philosophies, shape which factors and thus which moments are emphasized in the analysis. A strong bias toward particular strategies, such as overloads in possession, can distort the analysis by neglecting other decisive elements like timing. This simply stems from the complexity and diversity inherent to football. In this way, personal experience encourages subjective conclusions through the combination of the availability heuristic and WYSIATI.

    Industry observers note that the representativeness heuristic describes judgments about probability based on how representative something appears to be. Representativeness here refers to stereotypes and perceived similarity. When asked about probability, people often engage in substitution, evaluating plausibility instead of actual likelihood. Kahneman illustrates this with the following example:.

    “You see a person reading The Newly introduced York Times on the New York subway. Which of the following is a better bet about the reading stranger?

    She does not have a college degree.”.

    While the more plausible story might lead you to bet on the PhD, you should consider the base rates. Given that far more people without a college degree ride the New York subway than people with doctorates, the statistically sounder bet would be on the person not having a college degree. This example highlights the tension between base rate information and representativeness.

    “The representativeness heuristic is misleading when it causes people to ignore base rate information that points in a different direction.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Sources indicate that kahneman accordingly advises questioning the informativeness of data and anchoring probability judgments to plausible base rates. To further illustrate the relevance of this concept in a football context, consider the following recent example:.

    At the beginning of the 2024/25 season, Bayern Munich employed an aggressive, man-marking high press. This tactical approach faced heavy criticism, primarily due to the potential for conceding counterattack goals. Despite the fact that several clubs, such as Atalanta Bergamo, had already been successfully using man-marking in high pressing for years on the international stage, the approach was viewed as atypical in Germany. Since the 1990s, man-marking had largely been replaced in the Bundesliga by zonal marking or hybrid forms. The evaluation of Bayern’s pressing was guided by historical prototypes of man-marking, particularly those involving a libero and, thus, a structural numerical inferiority. Although the man-marking was implemented in a completely different tactical fashion, the comparison seemed plausible due to the similarity and influenced judgments about its success.

    In a recent development, in reality, the base rates painted a different picture: Bayern dominated their early Bundesliga matches, prevented opponents from gaining a foothold, and significantly limited their scoring opportunities. Statistically, the approach was highly successful: in their first 11 matches, 7 opponents failed to exceed an xG value of 0.5. The previous season’s champions, Leverkusen, only managed an xG of 0.17 and just 27% possession.

    Sources indicate that nonetheless, the assessment of Bayern’s man-marking pressing was distorted by the representativeness heuristic: instead of evaluating the actual likelihood of success based on objective data, the plausibility of an outdated playing style was used as the basis of judgment. This illustrates how stereotypical mental models can lead to misjudgments and how crucial it is to critically examine information in football analysis.

    For the sake of completeness, it should be mentioned that individual statistics (base rates in football) are not necessarily meaningful on their own. However, a combination of multiple statistics and data points can produce a more reliable picture to guide analysis. While xG values (as a combination of several data inputs) are still prone to error and need to be contextualized, they can nonetheless provide valuable insights into a team’s actual performance over time.

    The conjunction fallacy is one of the cognitive errors that arise from the representativeness heuristic. It describes the tendency of people to judge the combination of two events as more likely than one of the events alone, even when directly compared. The prerequisite is that the combination creates a more coherent and plausible story than the single event. One of the most controversial and well-known examples is the “Linda problem” by Kahneman and Tversky:.

    It has been revealed that “Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations.

    Which of the following is more probable?

    Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.”.

    In a recent development, despite the intuitive plausibility that Linda’s characteristics align more closely with the feminist movement, the first option is statistically more probable. After all, the conjunction of two events (“Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement”) is always less likely than one of the events alone (“Linda is a bank teller”).

    According to recent reports, „The most representative outcomes combine with the personality description to yield the most coherent stories. The most coherent stories are not necessarily the most probable, but they are plausible, and the concepts of coherence, plausibility, and probability are easily confused by the unwary.“ – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    The “less-is-more pattern” by Christopher Hsee ties into this problem. For those who want to read more, I’ve linked the relevant study here. It states that the probability of the broader event (e.g., Linda is a bank teller) must be higher than that of the event that is included within it (e.g., Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement). However, the more plausible event (less comprehensive) is judged to be more probable than the less plausible, more comprehensive one. This creates the “less-is-more” pattern. As a result, the probability estimate for the more detailed scenario is higher, even though this contradicts logical reasoning.

    “This is the trap for forecasters and their clients: the more detailed the scenarios, the more convincing they are, but the less probable they become.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Sources indicate that in the context of opponent team analysis for an upcoming match, the analyst must be aware that they are the forecaster, making probability estimates about the opponent’s future style of play. Thus, they should assess the likelihood of events, not merely their plausibility.

    Recent findings suggest that applying Hsee’s “less-is-more principle” to this context means that detailed, plausible match scenarios may sound impressive, but are statistically less reliable for prediction than broader descriptions. Each additional assumption in a forecast multiplies individual probabilities and thereby reduces the overall likelihood of an accurate prediction.

    However, this is not a call for a lack of detail in opponent analysis. On the contrary, the more detailed, precise, and comprehensive the analysis, the better the ability to derive general playing principles, patterns, and behaviors of the opponent. Therefore, the analyst should aim to analyze the opponent as holistically as possible before making generalized statements that increase the predictive probability.

    While in Part 2 I will address structural conditions in football that affect the intuition of analyst and coach experts, in this section I will focus on the individual conditions of different types of analysis. Even though I speak here about football analysis in general, it is notable to clarify that there are various forms of analysis in football (see table). Different types of analysis also have different individual susceptibilities to cognitive biases.

    Certain biases are additionally triggered by specific types of analysis. Prediction, for example, is particularly affected by the representativeness heuristic, since it involves assessing probabilities. Team analysis over multiple games increases susceptibility to the anchoring heuristic, and post-match analysis is prone to hindsight bias, the tendency to overestimate the predictability of an event after it has occurred.

    It has been revealed that similarly, focusing on a single level of analysis increases vulnerability to WYSIATI. You should now be familiar with the cognitive errors mentioned here, so they should not come as a surprise. One factor not yet addressed in this article, which demonstrably increases susceptibility to all biases, is time pressure. Time pressure plays a significant role especially during live analysis, though not exclusively.

    Time pressure forces analysts to make quicker decisions. Research reveals that under such conditions, people rely more heavily on heuristics, increasing the likelihood of errors. Among other studies, Finucane et al. (2000) examined the influence of the affect heuristic on the evaluation of benefits and risks, demonstrating that time pressure amplifies this effect.

    Analysts therefore have to rely more on their intuition during live analysis. This brings me to Part 2, where I will identify conditions that increase experts’ susceptibility to intuitive errors.

    By now, it should be clear why we delve so deeply into the mechanisms of heuristics. Without a fundamental understanding of how they work, heuristics and cognitive biases are difficult to recognize.

    According to recent reports, many behavioral psychology insights can be profitably applied in sports analysis. This includes not only heuristics and cognitive biases but can also be extended to other areas of football analysis. However, to cover these application areas sufficiently, there will be a Part 2, Part 3, and, if necessary, a Part 4.

    Recent findings suggest that in Part 2, I will address the topic of overconfidence. Among other things, it will examine the susceptibility of expert intuition as well as risk strategies and risk assessments in football. Strategies for avoiding biases in football analysis will also be presented.

    Industry observers note that part 3 (and possibly Part 4) will focus on “noise” in football analysis. Unlike bias, noise does not describe the distortion of judgments in a particular direction but the unconscious variability of multiple judgments under identical decision conditions.

    Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that ace left-hander Tarik Skubal, winner of the last two American League Cy Young awards and far and away the top free agent of the 2026-27 class, has agreed to terms with the Fresh York Mets on a nine-year contract worth $450 million, reports the New York Post. The deal has a $45 million signing bonus with no options or opt-outs, per SNY, as well as a full no-trade clause, so the Mets have locked Skubal up for the full nine years. Further, there are only $30 million in deferrals, according to the New York Post. The deal is pending a physical.

    Once finalized, the deal will make Skubal the highest-paid pitcher in Major League Baseball history, in terms of both total contract value and average annual salary.

    Skubal, who turned 30 years of age on Nov. 20, is the No. 1 ranked talent on our list of the top 50 free agents for this offseason. Here's part of Mike Axisa's write-up:.

    "Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He indicated few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself.".

    Industry observers note that over the last three seasons, Skubal has pitched to a 2.42 ERA and an FIP of 2.48 in 546 innings spread over 88 starts. That amounts to a total WAR of 17.7 since the start of the 2024 campaign. Skubal remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and this signing reflects that reality.

    Since Skubal was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the 2026 deadline, he was ineligible to receive the qualifying offer from the Dodgers. As such, the Mets will not be penalized a draft pick for signing Skubal.

    The nine years here aren't record-setting, as the longest pitcher contract remains the 12-year deal that Yoshinobu Yamamoto signed with the Dodgers. Yamamoto's $325 million was previously the largest contract for a pitcher -- obviously excepting Shohei Ohtani, as he's a two-way player -- so Skubal's $450 million shatters that record.

    According to recent reports, coming off a disappointing 88-loss campaign in 2026, the Mets, big-spending owner Steve Cohen, and lead decision-maker David Stearns needed to make an offseason splash to improve their chances of a 2027 rebound and inspire a perhaps disaffected fan base. Skubal more than qualifies. He'll front a Mets rotation that also includes 25-year-old right-hander Nolan McLean, who himself has frontline long-term potential. In Queens, Skubal joins a roster that also includes the All-Star likes of Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor, and Bo Bichette.

    It has been revealed that further, the Mets just locked up young outfielder A.J. Ewing to an eight-year, $95 million extension and we all know plenty about Soto's monster contract. The Mets now have Soto through 2039, Skubal through 2035, Ewing through 2034 and Lindor through 2031.

    The rotation for the Mets right now looks something like:.

    Given the large outlay for Skubal here, the Mets should be all-in on improving the ballclub for the 2027 season, which means we shouldn't expect them to stop with just signing Skubal. That last spot in the rotation, as such, should be ticketed to someone else outside the organization at present, whether a free agent or a trade acquisition.

    The landing of the top free agent available no doubt ramps up the pressure on Stearns and the Mets to deliver a playoff berth and a deep October run in 2027, but Skubal's presence also makes it much likely that such a feat comes to pass.

    Industry observers note that injuries have been one of the defining stories of the young 2026-27 NBA season, and while some teams like the Oklahoma City Thunder are unfortunately months away from relief, others are beginning to see a light at the end of the health tunnel. We're now nearly a month or so out from the early-season wave of losses, and on Friday, ESPN's Shams Charania gave updates on the health of several key absent players. Let's use that as a launching point to check in on a handful of injured stars.

    Industry observers note that it took Indiana's star point guard a full season to recover from the torn Achilles tendon he suffered in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, but sadly, his return lasted just four games before he headed back to the sideline. Haliburton was diagnosed with a left hamstring strain in October, and according to ESPN, he will be sidelined for at least the next couple of weeks.

    For now, there is no firmer timeline than that, with Pacers coach Rick Carlisle saying in a recent radio interview that he didn't think it was "out of the question" that Haliburton would play in November, but he would not "put a hard date on anything.".

    Haliburton looked mostly like himself in the four games he played early this season, averaging just under 22 points and 10 assists. The Pacers have fallen to 5-10 and the Eastern Conference's No. 10 seed without him, and they are seemingly aware of the need for reinforcements. The Pacers "clearly are looking at doing something" on the trade market, with an upgrade on the wing viewed as a strong possibility, Jake Fischer mentioned Friday on SiriusXM NBA Radio.

    Sources indicate that A return to action seems further off for Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards, who had knee surgery in late October. Edwards spoke with reporters Thursday and said he has "no clue" when he'll be able to return to the floor and declined to offer a timetable, per ESPN.

    Edwards missed 21 games last year and dealt with a knee issue in the postseason. Despite a hot start, that included a 47-point outburst against the Cavaliers, Edwards continued to experience discomfort in the knee, prompting the team to choose the surgery route rather than have their superstar continue playing through pain.

    "It needed to be done in order for me to be able to play without any pain for the next couple years," Edwards stated. "But who knows? Maybe in a couple years I might have to get something else. But hopefully not. I think I'll be pretty good.".

    Led by LaMelo Ball, the Wolves have excelled even in Edwards' absence. At 11-5, Minnesota sits at No. 5 in the Western Conference standings entering their game against the Grizzlies on Saturday.

    According to recent reports, leonard has played just twice this season due to knee swelling, but according to Charania, there is optimism that he will return within the next few weeks. Leonard has been dealing with patellar tendinopathy, more commonly known as "jumper's knee," TSN reported on Tuesday. That is the same concern he dealt with throughout his 2019 championship season. SportsNet confirmed that reporting, while noting that swelling is not typically how that injury presents. SportsNet's reporting indicates that the swelling and jumper's knee are separate issues.

    It has been revealed that the good news on this front is that the reporting to this point indicates that the Raptors do not expect these problems to linger once Leonard returns. Toronto successfully managed Leonard's health through that title season, and is being cautious to start this year as well. However, his absence has certainly been felt as Toronto is in the midst of a six-game losing streak without him.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, the player Leonard was traded for is just about ready to make his Clippers debut. Brandon Ingram is expected to return Monday against the Houston Rockets, according to Charania. Ingram suffered a partially torn Achilles tendon last season, which kept him out of the Clippers' lineup at the start of this year. His absence has been keenly felt in Los Angeles as the Clippers have scuttled to a 4-10 start without him. Los Angeles has both a bottom-eight offense and defense so far this season, so getting Ingram on the court should represent a helpful talent infusion.

    Industry observers note that san Antonio's second-year star thankfully avoided a major injury when he fell on the court against the Clippers on Thursday. He will, however, miss 1-3 weeks with a left hip rotator strain. Harper was walking without a limp following the injury, per The San Antonio Express-News, a positive sign for his recovery.

    According to recent reports, the Spurs have the NBA's best record at 13-3, but the story to watch as Harper rests is the performance of former All-Star De'Aaron Fox. Just beginning a four-year max contract, Fox has scored just 23 points in his last three games combined. He's averaging the fewest points and assists of his career since his rookie season. The Spurs had been starting their three high-profile guards -- Fox, Harper and Stephon Castle -- together early in the season. It was working, but with the caveat that that group never played a second without Victor Wembanyama. The Spurs are more than 40 points per 100 possessions better when their MVP candidate is on the floor.

    If Fox can't right the ship while Harper is out, that could open the door to San Antonio moving him to the bench upon Harper's return. The Spurs thrived last season with two ball-handlers, two shooters and Wembanyama in their starting lineup. The three guards are working because basically anything works with Wembanyama, but when the competition gets stiffer in the playoffs, it's going to be harder to get away with so little shooting in the starting lineup. That puts the onus on Fox to prove he still belongs in the starting lineup, and bouncing back while Harper is out will be a massive part of that.

    In a recent development, when it comes to the holidays, it's best to expect the unexpected. Rarely do things go smoothly when everyone convenes for Thanksgiving, so it's the right idea to lie back and simply roll with the punches as they come in. For instance, you have no idea what that weird uncle will say at the dinner table, nor can you guarantee the turkey won't be overcooked. It's bound to go off the rails in some capacity, but the one constant that you can lean on is that there will be football to help distract you from the madness, including the dog running outside with one of the turkey legs.

    Industry observers note that that mentioned, even the NFL is unpredictable, so it's up to us to try and see the forest through the trees and anticipate what could be on the horizon. Below, we're going to highlight a handful of storylines/individual performances from Week 12 that may surprise some people, but not us.

    All NFL odds courtesy of DraftKings Sportsbook.

    It was a modest day at the office for the entire Bears offense in Week 11, but they edged out a 21-13 win over the Saints. For his part, Colston Loveland was targeted just three times. The tight end hauled in all three passes for 29 yards, but did have a thunderous touchdown in the second quarter. That score should serve as the appetizer for a possible eye-popping performance from the Bears star pass catcher in Chicago's upcoming Thanksgiving matchup with the Detroit Lions.

    Recent findings suggest that this is the first of two matchups between these NFC North rivals this season, and first place in the division is hanging in the balance during this holiday contest. The Bears are a slight road favorite, and if they want to prove the oddsmakers right, featuring Loveland would go a long way in that endeavor.

    In Week 18 of last season (the last time Loveland played the Lions), the then rookie delivered arguably the best game of his career. He caught 10 of his 13 targets for 91 yards and a touchdown. Those receptions are still his career high. This season, the Lions have been extremely susceptible to tight ends, allowing the most receiving yards (740) and receiving touchdowns (11) to the position in the NFL. They're also giving up the third-most receptions (68) to the position group this season.

    This is a tasty matchup that Ben Johnson and organization should look to exploit to come out of Thanksgiving thankful for their ninth win of the season.

    Gambling angle to note: Colston Loveland's receiving yards prop for Week 12 is 54.5 (-109 to the Over). Loveland is +145 to score a touchdown.

    Recent findings suggest that the vibes surrounding the Rams have been off ever since they kicked off their season opener in Australia. A season marred by injury has seen this once-dubbed "superteam" enter its bye last week at 6-4, on the outside looking in on the playoff picture as the No. 9 seed. As they emerge from the break, however, there is an opportunity in front of them to climb back into the playoff picture, but they'll need a little help.

    According to recent reports, first and foremost, they'll need to take care of business during the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game where they host the Packers. Green Bay is right now clinging to the No. 7 seed in the NFL at 6-4 on the season. A mere win over the Packers on Wednesday would temporarily vault L.A. into the No. 7 seed. However, if they want to hold onto it coming out of Week 12 entirely, they'll need to hold their nose and root for the San Francisco 49ers to defeat the Seattle Seahawks at home.

    Sources indicate that that won't be a small feat as Seattle is coming off of its bye and the Niners are coming off an international game in Mexico City. That said, if San Francisco can fend off the defending champions, that'd create the necessary breathing room for the Rams to hold onto their spot in the playoff picture. If the Seahawks win, they'd draw even at 7-4 and retain the tiebreaker thanks to their superior divisional record. It's not an impossible needle to thread, but the Rams will need to get some help over the holiday weekend.

    Recent findings suggest that gambling angle to note: The Rams are -104 to make the playoffs. A Rams-49ers moneyline parlay pays out +159.

    A QB controversy has been brewing in the Pacific Northwest, specifically between Sam Darnold and Drew Lock. That talk about a QB controversy has been almost exclusively external, however, as the Seahawks have noted that Darnold -- who has missed the previous two games with rib and quad injuries -- will resume his role as QB1 when healthy. Head coach Mike Macdonald also noted that the team is optimistic that Darnold's return under center will come this week as they emerge from their bye and take on the San Francisco 49ers.

    According to recent reports, darnold has been sidelined for essentially four games so far (injured himself on the opening drive of the season opener), so we've seen what the offense looks like with Drew Lock at the helm. He's led Seattle to four wins (3-0 as the starter), while completing 73.1% of his passes and a 125.6 passer rating. By the numbers, Lock has outplayed Darnold from what we've seen so far in 2026, thus bringing up the question of whether or not to keep Lock as the starter.

    Industry observers note that again, Darnold will be the guy whenever he's ready to return, so there is no real controversy yet. However, if/when he returns this week, he might be set up for failure, as the 49ers are playing as well as any team in the NFL right now.

    If Darnold struggles and the Seahawks lose to the Niners to drop them to 6-5, that chatter to slot in Lock as QB1 will likely reach a fever pitch, particularly with the division and wild card races starting to slip away from them.

    I flagged this in my Cover 32 column for Week 11, but it's worth highlighting yet again. The Pittsburgh Steelers are dangerously close to seeing their season fall out from under them. They were 6-2 entering Week 9, and upon their return to the field, have looked nothing like the club that appeared destined to make the playoffs amid Aaron Rodgers' final season. Pittsburgh has dropped two straight games over the past two weeks, which now has them starting to fall down the wild card standings.

    Industry observers note that at 6-4, they're clinging to the No. 7 seed in the conference, which makes Friday's matchup at home against the Denver Broncos as close to a must-win as you'll find in Week 12. The Broncos are a 3-point road favorite in this game, so the oddsmakers are projecting Pittsburgh to fall to 6-5. If they do, they run dangerously close to falling out of the playoff picture entirely.

    It has been revealed that temporarily, that'd happen if the New England Patriots go to Los Angeles and beat the Los Angeles Chargers. New England would draw even at 6-5 with Pittsburgh but they own the head-to-head tiebreaker thanks to a Week 2 win. Of course, the Patriots will be without Drake Maye (fractured fibula), but things might be evened out on the QB front as Justin Herbert is presently in concussion protocol coming out of Week 11. That possibly sets up a Tommy DeVito vs. DJ Uiagalelei matchup that is a true coin flip.

    Industry observers note that while the Patriots could oust them from a playoff spot for this weekend, the bigger long-term concern is the Houston Texans. They are hosting the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday and are 6.5-point favorites. The double whammy for Pittsburgh would be for them to lose on Friday, see the Patriots beat the Chargers to shoot them down to the No. 8 seed, and then the Texans beat the Ravens to push them to 5-6. That's set up a Week 13 matchup between Pittsburgh and Houston that could very well be the nail in the coffin for their season if they don't turn things around.

    Gambling angle to note: A Texans, Patriots, Broncos moneyline parlay is +329.

    Recent findings suggest that it hasn't been the sophomore surge that folks hoped to see from Judkins this season, as the Browns back has struggled to be consistent. His 3.4 yards per carry average is a tick lower than his 3.6 yards per carry over his rookie season and is averaging just 47 rushing yards per game (59.1 yards per game in 14 games as a rookie in 2025). However, Cleveland's "Sunday Night Football" matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders set Judkins up with a true bounce-back opportunity.

    According to recent reports, the Raiders' run defense has been horrid so far in 2026. Coming into Week 12, Las Vegas is giving up the most rushing yards to running backs in the NFL this season (130.5 yards per game). Their 13 rushing touchdowns allowed are tied for the second-most in the league. The Raiders defense is coming off of a Week 11 loss to the Broncos, where rookie back Jonah Coleman steamrolled them for 111 yards on the ground and three rushing touchdowns.

    According to recent reports, as he enjoyed his bye week, Judkins was probably licking his chops seeing Coleman post those numbers, knowing full well that he'll get to face them this coming week. Judkins, a 2025 second-round pick, has rushed for at least 100 yards just once in his young career. Well, it wouldn't shock us if he not only notched his second-career game with 100 yards on the ground, but surpassed his 110-yard rushing game from Week 5 last season for a latest career-best mark. The Raiders have allowed a 100-yard rusher three times this season already.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • James Harden is in the midst of his worst scoring season since his second year in Oklahoma City 16 years ago, but the 37-year-old turned back the clock some on Friday night with a 51-point performance in a Cavaliers win over the Pacers.
    • Sources indicate that harden's vintage scoring night saw him go 15-of-26 from the field and 14-of-14 from the free-throw line in typical Harden fashion for the 26th 50-point game of his career.
    • At 37 years old (and 86 days), Harden is the fourth-oldest player to score 50 points in an NBA game, passing LeBron James on that list and trailing only Bryant, Jordan and Jamal Crawford, who scored 50 at 39 years old.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    James Harden is in the midst of his worst scoring season since his second year in Oklahoma City 16 years ago, but the 37-year-old turned back the clock some on Friday night with a 51-point performance in a Cavaliers win over the Pacers.

    Sources indicate that harden's vintage scoring night saw him go 15-of-26 from the field and 14-of-14 from the free-throw line in typical Harden fashion for the 26th 50-point game of his career. That moves him into third all-time in NBA history for 50-point games, passing Kobe Bryant and sitting just five behind Michael Jordan.

    At 37 years old (and 86 days), Harden is the fourth-oldest player to score 50 points in an NBA game, passing LeBron James on that list and trailing only Bryant, Jordan and Jamal Crawford, who scored 50 at 39 years old.

    After the game, Cavaliers' coach Kenny Atkinson offered an eyebrow-raising comment calling Harden "top-10 all-time," which drew immediate pushback from NBA fans, but Harden is an unquestioned Hall of Famer and continues to put his name among the all-time greats on NBA scoring lists.

    His co-star in Cleveland, Donovan Mitchell, lamented that Harden doesn't get the appreciation he deserves at this stage of his career, and that he expects, much like Russell Westbrook, that it won't happen until he retires.

    "He won't until it's over with," Mitchell said. "I hate it, but that's just the world we live in. We won't appreciate greatness. We didn't appreciate Russ in his latter years until now. It's like, 'Oh man, Russ was this and that.' It's like we forgot he averaged 28, 15 and 16 for a month. It's one of those things where we live in such a negative space. I hate it. At the end of the day, he doesn't care. And for me, seeing that, I don't care. It helps, but at the end of the day, that's just what the world is. It sucks that that's that way, but us in this locker room and guys in this league, we know who he is and we know what he's done for the game. That goes for not just him but a lot of people in this league. We don't appreciate what's in front of us on a consistent basis.".

    Harden has long been a divisive player among NBA fans. Some have appreciated his ruthless efficiency while others have hated the aesthetics of his mastery of the dark arts of drawing fouls. As Mitchell noted, few players have had as much influence over the game in the last decade-plus as Harden. From his massive stepback 3-pointer to his movement on drives to create contact, so much of Harden's game has made its way into the arsenal of most elite guard scorers.

    Fans will debate whether that's a good thing, but his influence is undeniable. As Mitchell said, whenever Harden calls it a career, he will get more appreciation, but there will also be heated debates over his place in NBA history as one of the most divisive stars (from a play-style perspective, at least) of his generation.

    6 lessons from Week 11: Kyle Shanahan is as good as it gets, plus a rookie RB earning a role

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, when I think about Thanksgiving, I think about going to my grandparents' house growing up.
    • According to recent reports, around midnight — sometimes later — we'd arrive at my grandparents' doorstep, weary but happy.
    • And then there was Thanksgiving Day, which meant football.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, when I think about Thanksgiving, I think about going to my grandparents' house growing up. We'd leave immediately after my dad got off work on Wednesday and drive from my hometown in rural Virginia to my mom's parents in Latest Jersey. A quick stop at the McDonald's was the only time we'd leave our route. We'd drive extra miles to avoid traffic. I'd try, often unsuccessfully, to fight off sleep on the drive up.

    According to recent reports, around midnight — sometimes later — we'd arrive at my grandparents' doorstep, weary but happy. They'd always greet us with smiling faces, no matter the hour.

    And then there was Thanksgiving Day, which meant football. My grandpa, a die-hard Giants fan, would lead our collective yelling at the TV, hoping the Cowboys would lose, and we'd pity-root for the Lions, who seemingly never won.

    According to recent reports, the results fade, but what I remember is my family being together. It wasn't perfect. It got harder as my grandparents got older. We'd laugh, we'd cheer, we'd wish it could last forever.

    In a recent development, it's been several years since then, but I still remember my grandparents waving us goodbye, my grandpa good-heartedly reminding my dad to go south, not north, on the turnpike. It felt like just minutes earlier, they had been standing in that doorway welcoming us in. It always went too fast.

    Recent findings suggest that so ahead of our six lessons, let me give you a non-football one: Try to cherish this week. If you can do it with family, great. If you can do it with friends, great. If all you can do is call or text, great. It doesn't have to be perfect. Whether you watch every football game this week or none at all, I hope you're surrounded by people you love.

    In a recent development, coach of the Year has become so misconstrued, and not just in the NFL. Every individual player award honors the best player, but for some reason Coach of the Year honors the coach whose team exceeds expectations most.

    Sources indicate that so, once again, Kyle Shanahan's magnificent job will likely go unrewarded, simply because he's done too good a job for too long. An early congratulations to either John Harbaugh or Todd Monken for winning. They've done magnificent jobs.

    But Kyle Shanahan is the best coach in the NFL this season. The 49ers just dismantled the Vikings to move to 9-1. They have won games in Australia and Mexico and Seattle and Dallas, all places with their own unique challenges. They have won games using wide receivers they never imagined having to count on.

    Sources indicate that thought you saw the best of Brock Purdy? Think again. I've written at length about why Purdy deserves MVP and is much more than just a product of the Shanahan system, but there's no doubt Shanahan has raised his game immensely. This offense is so well-constructed, so prepared for each and every task each and every week and so connected.

    The Vikings love to blitz. Purdy shredded them with quick passes: 12-for-13 for 161 yards and two touchdowns on throws released in 2.5 seconds or faster. Minnesota entered the night leading the NFL in sack rate and pressure rate. It managed just one sack and a 29% pressure rate, both season lows.

    This is nothing latest, by the way.

    Oh yeah, and Shanahan also made the excellent hire of defensive coordinator Raheem Morris, who has helped turn this defense from quite poor to elite.

    Recent findings suggest that it's silly that we'll look back and likely see someone else win Coach of the Year. Shanahan has never won the award, by the way, even though he's been the best or among the best in the profession for nearly a decade. Andy Reid, who's fourth all-time in wins, has won it once, back in 2002 with the Eagles. Sean McVay has won it once since becoming a head coach in 2017. Kevin Stefanski, a perfectly solid coach but nothing more, has won it twice.

    Recent findings suggest that again, even if he doesn't win "Coach of the Year," Shanahan is very much the defining coach of this year. He'd gladly take a Lombardi Trophy over any individual award, anyway.

    One day after Brian Flores' normally excellent defense was shredded, one of his disciplines had his best performance yet. Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones and his unit were terrific in a 22-20 upset win over the Bengals.

    Jones, like Flores, brings extra pressure, massive time. Washington is third in blitz rate this year. Joe Burrow has destroyed blitzes all year, but on Monday night, not so much.

    Jones was without his best cornerback, Amik Robertson, but refused to back down. His corners played physically, aggressively and well. The safeties followed in kind. And while Cincinnati's running game has never been a strength, Washington turned it into a decided weakness. The Bengals' 14% rushing success rate was the worst by any team in any game this year.

    According to recent reports, jones has this defense moving in the right direction, too. In November, the Commanders rank 15th in defensive EPA per play; they were 23rd before that. They've done a good job stopping the run and limiting explosives, largely because they have the third-lowest missed tackle rate in the league. Washington hasn't allowed more than 23 points in a game since Week 5.

    There will be significant-picture coaching questions in Washington if the team doesn't make the playoffs, but Jones has done solid work under the radar.

    According to recent reports, I wrote about this in our Week 11 overreactions, but the Steelers are once again a team with a winning record and little chance of winning a playoff game. Here, though, let's talk about the style.

    Aaron Rodgers is now completing 21.6% of his passes thrown 20+ yards downfield. While he is throwing way more of them this year — only Jordan Love has more than Rodgers' 51 attempts — they're mostly performative "See? I'll still take shots downfield" throws that are low-percentage floaters. Only Cam Ward and recently released Daniel Jones have a lower completion rate on these throws.

    Sources indicate that the run game can be quite good. In fact, the Steelers are second in rushing EPA per play this year at 0.06. Earlier in the season, it seemed they finally had one truly sterling offensive aspect. This made them different.

    In a recent development, but when the run game isn't going well, as has been the case the last two weeks, Pittsburgh has nothing else. The Steelers are 4-0 when their EPA per rush is above their overall season mark and 2-4 when it is below it. Pittsburgh was at -0.19, second-worst of the season, in the Week 11 loss to the Eagles.

    The Steelers have been the same as they've been during this playoff win drought: poor quarterbacking, good-not-great defense.

    K. Pickett, M. Rudolph, M. Trubisky.

    Just a dull, stuck-going-nowhere team archetype and a franchise that seems fine with it.

    The Chiefs' three-game winning streak has coincided with a soft schedule. There's not a ton to take away from it in terms of Kansas City's standing in the championship-contending pecking order.

    According to recent reports, but on an individual level, Emmett Johnson is a beast. In his two starts with Kenneth Walker III out, Johnson has 134 yards from scrimmage and three touchdowns.

    Industry observers note that emmett Johnson has now recorded back to back 100 yard rushing games since taking over for Kenneth Walker.23 CAR, 105 RUSH YDS, 1 TD, 4 REC, 38 REC YDS vs Cardinals.Johnson's OROY chances have skyrocketed over the last two weeks. https://t.co/dt5FdKVwLi pic.twitter.com/tNep8zsuxb.

    Johnson currently leads all running backs in 7.0 yards per touch (min. 50 touches). He also leads all running backs in tackle avoidance rate (36.8), which is also first and slightly higher than tackle-avoiding machine Walker III.

    Industry observers note that johnson has a true three-down skill set. Only 11.3% of his rushes go for 0 or negative yards, the fourth-lowest rate among all running backs with at least 50 touches, and he has turned several potential losses into gains.

    Sources indicate that walker is a stud. He'll be the feature back when he returns from his groin injury. But Johnson has proved he not only deserves a legit complementary role down the stretch and beyond, but with his pass-catching acumen, he can actually be a weapon, too.

    Sources indicate that the Colts got thumped 26-3 by the Texans on Thursday, and that somehow wasn't the worst aspect of their week. Not even close.

    Recent findings suggest that one day after that, Indianapolis released Daniel Jones, and shortly after that, reports surfaced that at the trade deadline, the Colts had turned down the Ravens' offer of a fourth-and fifth-round pick for Jones (the fifth would be returned if Baltimore made the playoffs). Now, they get nothing for Jones and will carry a $35.2 million dead cap hit in 2027.

    Industry observers note that if interim GM Ed Dodds wasn't already filling in for a fired GM (Chris Ballard), this would be a fireable offense. Maybe it is, anyway. The Colts sold away many of their franchise pillars but stopped at Daniel Jones?

    According to various reports, the Colts turned away multiple suitors for Jones, including Baltimore's potentially lucrative one; multiple suitors for Jonathan Taylor, who fetched offers for a second-round pick plus more; at least one offer that included a fourth-round pick for veteran defensive tackle Grover Stewart, who's 33 and in a contract year.

    Recent findings suggest that I gave the Colts a D+ in my trade deadline grades and, upon first reflection, thought I might have been a little harsh. Indianapolis did get decent draft capital back for the moves it did make. But now, I think that mark might be generous. Every meaningless hard hit Taylor takes, and every meaningless double-team Stewart takes on, is just that. Meaningless.

    In a recent development, the Colts have very little young, cost-controlled talent. They don't have their first-round pick in 2027. They will have a new GM and, likely, a new coach. They are arguably the worst team in the NFL in 2026. They will be in the running for worst team in the NFL in 2027 and potentially 2028. They just turned down draft capital for a player they didn't even want. If there were a class in mismanaging an enterprise worth billions of dollars, the Colts' front office could do a great job teaching it.

    If it feels like there's been a little bit of a midseason lull, it's because there has been. In November, there's been a ton of blowouts — seven games decided by 15+ every week from Week 8-10, and then a lot of byes and semi-competitive games in Week 11.

    But the league is cranking it up a notch this coming week.

    Industry observers note that the Bears have won five straight, but their last two are over the lowly Buccaneers and Saints, with a bye in between. The Lions have won six straight, but the last three are over the Dolphins, the Patriots (mostly without Drake Maye) and the Buccaneers. I'm a huge believer in "you can only beat who's on your schedule." But in terms of learning about these teams, the past few weeks haven't been very helpful.

    That all changes this week. On Thanksgiving, the 8-2 Lions host the 8-2 Bears (on CBS and streaming on Paramount+, by the way!), which should be an absolute banger.

    This is far from the only example. Get your nap in early, because later that night, Chiefs at Bills is a can't-miss. Buffalo has seemed almost bored — and certainly hasn't been very sharp — in wins over the Ravens, Carson Wentz-led Vikings, Jets and Dolphins. But they'll absolutely be locked in against their bitter rival. The Chiefs, meanwhile, have cruised past the Jets, Falcons and Saints after a tough loss to the Broncos. We have questions about Josh Allen's turnovers, Patrick Mahomes' deep-passing renaissance — is it real or fake? — and much more.

    #187779. Chat GPT: Diagonality Football’s Hidden Dimension of Play

    📅 12 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 50m • 📚 Deep Dive (10066 w)
